bibleSpine.kjv: And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit. Howbeit that was not first which is spiritual, but that which is natural; and afterward that which is spiritual. The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.
bibleSpine.gloss: The section's title text: Christ is the LAST/SECOND Adam, standing where the first man fell. He entered the same arena as the first Adam — a real man of flesh (v.47 the second man), yet the quickening Spirit who reverses the ruin.

bibleSpine.kjv: For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
bibleSpine.gloss: Two representative men, two heads of the race. Adam's ONE disobedience made many sinners; the second Adam's obedience makes many righteous. The contrast is obedience vs. disobedience in the same fallen arena — not two different natures.

bibleSpine.kjv: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.
bibleSpine.gloss: MADE OF A WOMAN, MADE UNDER THE LAW. He entered the human line by ordinary descent from a fallen woman, and stood under the law's curse where guilty man stood — the only way to redeem those under it.

bibleSpine.kjv: Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh;
bibleSpine.gloss: MADE OF THE SEED OF DAVID ACCORDING TO THE FLESH. Not a manufactured, sinless-Adam body but the actual fallen lineage of David — David who said 'in sin did my mother conceive me' (Ps. 51:5). The flesh Christ took was that hereditary stream, four thousand years down from Eden.

bibleSpine.kjv: For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh:
bibleSpine.gloss: The core text. God sent His Son in the LIKENESS OF SINFUL FLESH — not the likeness of sinless flesh, and not a mere appearance. He took the actual fallen flesh and there, IN THE FLESH, condemned sin by never once yielding to it.

bibleSpine.kjv: That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
bibleSpine.gloss: The PURPOSE of v.3: because Christ met and mastered sin in the very flesh we bear, the law's righteousness can now be fulfilled in us who walk after the Spirit. His victory in fallen flesh is the pledge of ours.

bibleSpine.kjv: Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. For verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham. Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.
bibleSpine.gloss: He TOOK PART OF THE SAME flesh and blood as the children — not angel-nature, but the SEED OF ABRAHAM. IN ALL THINGS it behoved him to be MADE LIKE UNTO HIS BRETHREN. 'The same' and 'in all things' bar every escape hatch that would give Him a different, unfallen humanity.

bibleSpine.kjv: For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.
bibleSpine.gloss: His temptation was REAL suffering, not a staged demonstration. Only genuine temptation in genuine fallen flesh qualifies Him to succour the tempted — a sinless-Adam nature would leave Him unable to feel our struggle.

bibleSpine.kjv: For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.
bibleSpine.gloss: The double guard in one verse: IN ALL POINTS TEMPTED LIKE AS WE ARE (full identity of nature and temptation) — YET WITHOUT SIN (absolute sinlessness). Nature fully ours; sin never His. Both held with equal force.

bibleSpine.kjv: Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered; And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him;
bibleSpine.gloss: The difference between Christ and us is the LIFE lived in the flesh, not the flesh. He LEARNED obedience by suffering and was 'made perfect' — a real moral warfare won by unbroken surrender, making Him the author of salvation to all who likewise obey.

bibleSpine.kjv: And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.
bibleSpine.gloss: Born of a fallen woman by ordinary conception, yet that which was born is called HOLY — the Son of God. The nature was ours; the character, from conception, was without sin. Both truths spoken by the angel in one breath.

bibleSpine.kjv: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
bibleSpine.gloss: The Word was MADE FLESH — real, present, dwelling flesh — not clothed in a phantom body. He entered the same flesh the children of men wear, and in it manifested the Father's glory.

bibleSpine.kjv: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
bibleSpine.gloss: He emptied Himself, took the servant's form, was MADE IN THE LIKENESS OF MEN, and in that humanity was OBEDIENT unto death. The condescension is into real, humbled humanity; the triumph is His obedience within it.

bibleSpine.kjv: For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
bibleSpine.gloss: Prophecy of the nature He took: no outward advantage, a root out of DRY GROUND, a man of sorrows acquainted with grief. He wore humanity at its weakest and most unlovely — degenerate flesh, not glorified Adam-flesh.

bibleSpine.kjv: For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
bibleSpine.gloss: The strongest guard of both truths together: God MADE HIM TO BE SIN for us (He took the full weight of fallen flesh and the sinner's condemnation) — WHO KNEW NO SIN (He never once consented). Made to be sin; knew no sin. Nature and character held apart.

bibleSpine.kjv: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth:
bibleSpine.gloss: The sinlessness guard stated absolutely: in the fallen flesh He bore, He DID NO SIN, not once. Consent never came. The nature was ours; the record is spotless.

symbolDefs.meaning: Christ as the new head and representative of the human race, standing where the first Adam fell — but in FALLEN flesh rather than unfallen, and rendering unbroken obedience where the first man rendered disobedience. The whole point of the figure is a real re-run of Adam's probation in the actual condition of Adam's ruined descendants, so that His obedience can be reckoned to the many just as Adam's disobedience was.
receipts: 1 Corinthians 15:45 — 'the last Adam was made a quickening spirit'; the last/second Adam is set over against the first as the reversing head of the race
1 Corinthians 15:47 — 'the second man is the Lord from heaven'
Romans 5:19 — 'by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous'; two heads, contrasted only by obedience vs. disobedience
Hebrews 2:16-17 — He took the seed of Abraham and was 'made like unto his brethren' in all things, i.e. He took His stand inside fallen humanity, not above it

symbolDefs.meaning: the fallen, hereditary, degenerate human nature — weakened by four thousand years of sin, subject to infirmity and temptation from within and without — which Christ actually took (the LIKENESS OF SINFUL FLESH meaning real fallen flesh, not a mere appearance of it), and in which He never once consented to sin. 'Sinful flesh' names the nature He bore; it never names any sin He committed, for nature is not sin and His consent never came.
receipts: Romans 8:3 — 'God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh'; the flesh is sinful flesh, yet sin is condemned IN it, not committed by Him
Romans 1:3 — 'made of the seed of David according to the flesh'; the flesh is the actual fallen Davidic lineage (cf. Ps. 51:5)
Hebrews 2:14 — 'he also himself likewise took part of the same' flesh and blood as the children
Hebrews 4:15 — 'in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin'; the flesh is fully ours (tempted like as we are) yet the life is sinless
2 Corinthians 5:21 — 'made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin'; the reckoning of sinful flesh laid on Him, while He knew no sin

witnesses.author: E. J. Waggoner
witnesses.quote: the fact that Christ took upon Himself the flesh, not of a sinless being, but of a sinful man, that is, that the flesh which He assumed had all the weaknesses and sinful tendencies to which fallen human nature is subject, is shown by the statement that He 'was made of the seed of David according to the flesh.' David had all the passions of human nature. He says of himself, 'Behold I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.' Psalm 51:5.
witnesses.gloss: Waggoner in 'Christ and His Righteousness' defines the flesh Christ took directly from Rom. 1:3 / Rom. 8:3 — not a sinless Adam-body but flesh with 'all the weaknesses and sinful tendencies to which fallen human nature is subject.' The section's thesis stated by the pioneer, grounded on Scripture.

witnesses.author: E. J. Waggoner
witnesses.quote: Likeness of Sinful Flesh.—There is a common idea that this means that Christ simulated sinful flesh; that he did not take upon himself actual sinful flesh, but only what appeared to be such. But the Scriptures do not teach such a thing... He took the same flesh that all have who are born of woman. A parallel text to Romans 8:3, 4 is found in 2 Corinthians 5:21.
witnesses.gloss: 'Waggoner on Romans' closes the phantom-flesh escape hatch: 'likeness of sinful flesh' is not simulation; He took 'the same flesh that all have who are born of woman' — and ties Rom. 8:3 to 2 Cor. 5:21 exactly as the Bible spine does.

witnesses.author: E. J. Waggoner
witnesses.quote: Even so Christ came in the same sinful flesh, yet he was without sin, because he was always led by the Spirit.
witnesses.gloss: The definitive resolution of both truths in one sentence: SAME sinful flesh, YET without sin — and the reason is the life He lived ('always led by the Spirit'), not a different nature. Exactly the section's guard.

witnesses.author: A. T. Jones
witnesses.quote: He was made in the likeness of men, as men are, just where they are. 'The Word was made flesh.' He 'took part of the same' flesh and blood as that of which the children of men are partakers, as they are since man has fallen into sin. And so it is written: 'When the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth His Son, made ... under the law.'
witnesses.gloss: Jones in 'The Consecrated Way to Christian Perfection' walks Phil. 2, John 1:14, Heb. 2:14 and Gal. 4:4 together: Christ took 'the same' flesh and blood 'as they are since man has fallen into sin,' made under the law where guilty man stood.

witnesses.author: A. T. Jones
witnesses.quote: Perfection, perfection of character, is the Christian goal—perfection attained in human flesh in this world. Christ attained it in human flesh in this world and thus made and consecrated a way by which, in Him, every believer can attain it.
witnesses.gloss: Jones names the fruit of the doctrine: Christ attained perfection of character IN human flesh, opening the same road for the believer — the difference is the life lived in the flesh, and that life is reproducible.

witnesses.author: A. T. Jones
witnesses.quote: There is a mystery in how God can be manifest in such sinful flesh as yours.
witnesses.gloss: Jones in 'Lessons on Faith' presses the point personally — God manifest in 'such sinful flesh as yours' — the same flesh Christ took, the ground of the believer's hope.

witnesses.author: Ellen G. White
witnesses.quote: It would have been an almost infinite humiliation for the Son of God to take man's nature, even when Adam stood in his innocence in Eden. But Jesus accepted humanity when the race had been weakened by four thousand years of sin. Like every child of Adam He accepted the results of the working of the great law of heredity.
witnesses.gloss: The four-thousand-years statement: Christ did NOT take Adam's unfallen Eden nature; He accepted humanity weakened by four thousand years of sin, taking the results of heredity 'like every child of Adam.'

witnesses.author: Ellen G. White
witnesses.quote: For four thousand years the race had been decreasing in physical strength, in mental power, and in moral worth; and Christ took upon Him the infirmities of degenerate humanity... But our Saviour took humanity, with all its liabilities. He took the nature of man, with the possibility of yielding to temptation.
witnesses.gloss: Christ took 'the infirmities of DEGENERATE humanity' and 'the nature of man, with the possibility of yielding to temptation' — real fallen flesh, real conflict, or He could not stand in Adam's place.

witnesses.author: Ellen G. White
witnesses.quote: Christ, who knew not the least taint of sin or defilement, took our nature in its deteriorated condition.
witnesses.gloss: Both truths in one line: 'knew not the least taint of sin' (character) yet 'took our nature in its deteriorated condition' (nature). The deteriorated nature is ours; the defilement never His.

witnesses.author: Ellen G. White
witnesses.quote: In taking upon Himself man's nature in its fallen condition, Christ did not in the least participate in its sin. He was subject to the infirmities and weaknesses by which man is encompassed... He was touched with the feeling of our infirmities, and was in all points tempted like as we are. And yet He knew no sin.
witnesses.gloss: The chapter titled 'Sinlessness of Christ's Human Nature' holds the exact balance the section requires: fallen nature ('man's nature in its fallen condition,' subject to infirmity) with absolute non-participation in sin ('did not in the least participate in its sin').

witnesses.author: Ellen G. White
witnesses.quote: He could have sinned; He could have fallen, but not for one moment was there in Him an evil propensity.
witnesses.gloss: The guard-statement quoted honestly: the temptation was real ('He could have sinned; He could have fallen'), and the sinlessness was total ('not for one moment... an evil propensity'). This is about consent and character, not an unfallen nature.

witnesses.author: Ellen G. White
witnesses.quote: Jesus revealed no qualities, and exercised no powers, that men may not have through faith in Him. His perfect humanity is that which all His followers may possess, if they will be in subjection to God as He was.
witnesses.gloss: The difference is the life, not the nature: Christ exercised 'no powers that men may not have through faith in Him,' and His perfect humanity 'all His followers may possess' by the same subjection to God — the section's closing conviction.

witnesses.author: Ellen G. White
witnesses.quote: But many say that Jesus was not like us, that He was not as we are in the world, that He was divine, and that we cannot overcome as He overcame. But Paul writes, 'Verily he took not on him the nature of angels; but he took on him the seed of Abraham. Wherefore in all things it behooved him to be made like unto his brethren...'
witnesses.gloss: Ellen White answers the very objection this section confronts — 'many say Jesus was not like us' — by driving straight to Heb. 2:16-17: He took the seed of Abraham, made like His brethren in all things, that we may overcome as He overcame.

historyAnchor: Waggoner (CHR 1890) and Jones (CWCP 1905) developed this from the 1888 Minneapolis message on righteousness by faith, and Ellen White's strongest guard-statements (1SM 253-256; the 1895 'be careful how you dwell upon the human nature of Christ' letter behind FLB 49.4) come from the same 1890s controversy.
uncertainties: FLB 49.4 (and the parallel 5BC 1128 / 7ABC 447 'Baker letter') is a real EGW guard-statement, but note it also warns 'Do not set Him before the people as a man with the propensities of sin' and calls Him 'the second Adam' whose divine nature the Godhead pledged — cite it for the sinlessness/consent guard, not to imply an unfallen nature; keep the whole balance.

The task brief mentioned DA 671-672 and COL 311-319; I did not verify or include them since the DA 48-49, 117, 664 and 1SM/CWCP/CHR/WOR passages already carry the argument with verified text. They can be added if the writer wants more density, but each must be re-verified before citing.
